subject_line: A Canadian expatriate's travels in Soft Power
email_body:
Dear Stewart,

I came to Soft Power through its description as a collection shaped by travel and displacement, drawing on your life as a Canadian expatriate in the US Midwest, and I was struck by The Fiddlehead's phrase that it is political without being prescriptive. I'd be curious to hear how teaching in Oshkosh has changed the way you look back at Canada, and whether the insomnia-haunted questions of Questions in Bed still find their way into your newer poems.

book_title: Every Day We Live Is the Future: Surviving in a City of Disasters
subject_line: Five years beside Lake Managua with Dayani and Yadira
email_body:
Dear Douglas,

Every Day We Live Is the Future stayed with me for its patience: five years following Dayani Baldelomar and Yadira Castellón after they left rural Nicaragua, with Dayani settling in The Widows, a shantytown squeezed between a drainage ditch and Lake Managua. I'd love to ask how you negotiated that long relationship with two families, and how you decided where your own presence belonged on the page.

subject_line: Renovating a house with a history in Dream House
email_body:
Dear Valerie,

I was intrigued to learn that Dream House grew out of your own experience renovating a house that had been the site of a homicide, and that Separate Kingdoms later carried your stories between the United States and Russia, drawing on your time in Eastern Europe. I would like to ask how lived experience becomes fiction for you, what you kept from that house, and how your interest in disability studies now shapes the stories you write and teach in Milwaukee.

subject_line: Queerness on Missouri's working-class outskirts in SISSY
email_body:
Dear Canese,

I came to SISSY through the Colorado Review, which reads it as a book about the struggle of what it means to be queer in the working-class outskirts of Missouri. Having followed the line from your chapbook dark acre with Willow Springs Books to this Garden-Door Press debut, I'd love to ask how the rural landscapes of the chapbook grew into the full collection, and what writing so close to home in Missouri makes possible or difficult.

subject_line: Virgin martyrs and true crime in Other Girls to Burn
email_body:
Dear Caroline,

Other Girls to Burn sets early Christian virgin martyrs beside modern true crime, the 2014 Isla Vista shooting and mixed martial arts, held together by a thread of female mystics. I noticed the title phrase already surfacing in your 2014 Conjunctions essay "I Am a Burning Girl," and I'd love to ask how long that line travelled with you before it became a book, and how editing Pleiades now shapes the way you read the essay form.

I'd love to ask how you decided to leave the city and country unnamed, and how that early Milkweed National Fiction Prize book looks to you now from your classroom in Warrensburg.

subject_line: From Peru, Indiana to the stage: The Circus in Winter
email_body:
Dear Cathy,

The Circus in Winter has had an unusual second life: a traveling circus wintering in Peru, Indiana, became a musical written by fourteen Ball State students with Beth Turcotte and Ben Clark, then played the International Circus Hall of Fame, opened and closed the NAMT festival, and reached Goodspeed. I'd love to ask what it was like to watch your stories reshaped by students you might have taught, and what you learned about the book from seeing it sung.

email_body:

I've been reading about your path from the 2016 Finishing Line Press chapbook Play, whose poems range from love and mortality to good and evil, to your full-length collection A Dangerous Heaven from Gnashing Teeth Publishing. I was interested that you serve as poet laureate of the Pee Dee region while teaching at Francis Marion. I'd love to ask what that public role asks of your poems, and whether Florence and the Pee Dee find their way into A Dangerous Heaven.

subject_line: Fishing, memory and the inlet, from Winter Inlet to Ballyhoo
email_body:
Dear Hastings,

Winter Inlet was described as a lyrical and gritty portrait of coastal life, tying memory to fishing and the ocean, and I enjoyed Carrie Shipers' reading of "Winter Inlet Arrangement" in 32 Poems as a sonnet that refuses the usual Petrarchan resolution. With Ballyhoo following from Johns Hopkins University Press, I'd love to ask how living and teaching near Murrells Inlet continues to shape your lines, and whether that refusal of tidy resolution still guides how you end a poem.

book_title: See It Feelingly: Classic Novels, Autistic Readers, and the Schooling of a No-Good English Professor
subject_line: Six co-readers and the classics in See It Feelingly
email_body:
Dear Ralph,

See It Feelingly stays with me for its structure: rather than arguing in the abstract, you read classic novels alongside six autistic co-readers, testing the assumption of autistic literalness that your son DJ and autistic bloggers had already challenged. Reviewers have noted how the book mixes neuroscience, criticism, autistic poetry and neurodiversity politics. I'd love to ask which of those reading sessions most changed your own sense of a novel, and how that experience now shapes your poetry and teaching at Grinnell.

subject_line: From Oklahoma to Anne Askew in Prize for the Fire
email_body:
Dear Rilla,

After novels so rooted in Oklahoma, from the oil-boom racial violence of Fire in Beulah to the family caught up in new immigration legislation in Kind of Kin, I was struck that Prize for the Fire travels to sixteenth-century England and the martyr Anne Askew. I'd love to ask what drew you across that distance in time and place, and whether writing about a woman persecuted for her convictions felt connected to the Oklahoma questions of conscience your earlier books take on.

book_title: Carry: A Memoir of Survival on Stolen Land
subject_line: Snapshots of land and violence in Carry
email_body:
Dear Toni,

Carry moves through your life in snapshots, linking school shootings to racism and assault on campus in the title essay, and following women's peril at the Standing Rock pipeline protests in "Women in the Fracklands." Its writing about violence against Indigenous women and land, and how that violence is hidden and forgotten, stayed with me. I'd love to ask how you arrived at that fragmented structure, and how your Métis identity shapes the way you now teach creative writing in Arkansas.

subject_line: Realism meets the fantastic in The Age of Discovery
email_body:
Dear Becky,

Reading about The Age of Discovery and Other Stories, I was interested that your fourth collection mixes realism and the fantastic, after Scavengers stayed closer to ordinary losses, like the woman who turns to reality TV after losing her job, or the man in "The Lake" facing his father's possible dementia. I'd love to ask what opened the door to the fantastic in this book, and whether the dark humor reviewers noticed in Scavengers changes when the rules of the world loosen.

email_body:

The Bower, begun during your Fulbright year in Northern Ireland, follows a speaker's year in Belfast with her young daughter, viewing the legacy of sectarian violence through a visiting North American family. I noticed you now divide your life between Las Cruces and Belfast and read in Armagh this July. I would love to ask how southern New Mexico and the streets of Belfast talk to each other in your work, and what the outsider view allowed you to see.

email_body:
Dear Abraham,

I noticed that Surgencies, your book-length ode to rural Wisconsin from Baobab Press, follows Insomniac Sentinel and the 81-page long poem Dear Weirdo, which the Wisconsin Academy heard as your own voice set within a chorus of voices across space and time. Since you grew up in Ladysmith and now write and teach in Ogden, I'd love to ask what writing an ode to Wisconsin from Utah makes possible, and whether your time as Ogden's poet laureate changed how you think about place.

subject_line: The trobairitz, Interim and We Step into the Sea
email_body:
Dear Claudia,

Looking at your work in recent years, I was struck by its range: We Step into the Sea gathers new and selected poems from Barrow Street, Ecstatic Émigré came out from the University of Michigan Press, and your Truth of My Songs brought the poems of the trobairitz into English for Omnidawn. I'd love to ask how translating those medieval women poets has changed your own lines, and what editing Interim from Las Vegas has taught you about the poetry of the moment.
